deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. Folio 130 continues a German prose narrative of ancient history, the campaign of Alexander the Great, carried over from folio 129 (siege of Tyre, Egypt) and continued on folio 131 (Arbela, Babylon, Susa, Persepolis). The handwriting and style suggest lecture notes or a school exercise on universal history; they may not be by Gauss himself. The page relates the following:

- Alexander treated the Egyptians well and gave them governors (Statthalter) from their own country.
- He made the expedition to the oracle of Jupiter Ammon and then marched into Asia.
- The march met few obstacles. He did not need to carry provisions because the lands he passed through were mostly rich (reading uncertain, see corrections).
- The Asian nations submitted without resistance. He crossed the Euphrates near Circesium (reading uncertain), and in 331 BC crossed the Tigris.
- Meanwhile Darius had assembled an army of 600,000 men.
- They met in old Assyria. The terrain now favoured Darius as much as it had favoured Alexander at Issus.
- On 1 October 331 they met, and on the following day Alexander won a complete victory with 47,000 troops. Folio 131 names the battle as Arbela, i.e. Gaugamela.

There is no derivation, formula, computation or mathematical problem to reconstruct. The only numbers are historical dates and troop counts.
errors: The date sequence is internally loose. The text says the armies met on 1 October 331 and Alexander won 'am folgenden Tag'. The battle of Gaugamela is conventionally dated to 1 October 331 BC, so the victory would fall on 2 October by this account. This is a minor historical imprecision, not a mathematical error.
The crossing of the Euphrates is usually placed at Thapsacus rather than Circesium, if 'Circesium' is the correct reading.
Darius's army of 600,000 is one of several divergent ancient figures; Arrian gives about 1,000,000. Alexander's 47,000 matches Arrian's 40,000 infantry plus 7,000 cavalry.
deep.surprise_reason: The page is purely historical prose on Alexander the Great's campaign up to Gaugamela, apparently lecture or school notes. It contains no mathematical content at all, so there is nothing that could be attributed to Gauss as a result.

checkable.asserts: Alexander's army at Gaugamela per Arrian (40,000 infantry + 7,000 cavalry) equals the 47,000 troops stated on the page (trivial consistency check).

transcription_corrections: Line 5-6: 'weil die meisten {+r+}eichen[?] {+L+}änder waren durch die erkannt[?]' should most likely read 'weil es meistens reiche Länder waren, durch die er kam'. 'durch die er kam' fits the visible letters and the sense far better than 'erkannt'; the blue superscript corrections r/L adjust 'reiche'/'Länder'.
Line 2: the interlinear insertion above 'Zug' is 'einen', giving 'unternahm er einen Zug zum Orakel des Jupiter Ammon'.
Line 8: 'bei Circesium' is plausible from the image but remains uncertain.
Line 10: 'zu sam-men gebracht' is a hyphenation across lines, i.e. 'zusammengebracht'.
Line 3: 'Sein Marsch war' is confirmed by the image.
